newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysian derivatives blossom as markets reel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysian derivatives blossom as markets reel.

text.p: One man's ruin became another man's reward in Malaysia last week when nervous investors seeking havens from volatile regional stock and currency markets snapped up derivatives.
For the country's young futures exchanges, the volatility in the stock and currency markets seemed heaven-sent after months of moribund volumes.

Economic concerns in Thailand battered the baht and spread to neighbours including Malaysia, whose share market dropped nearly six percent last week. Thai stocks sank 7.3 percent over the same period.

"A lot more people are talking about our markets," John Lee, general manager of the 1-1/2 year old Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange (KLOFFE), told a derivatives conference here this week.

KLOFFE trades futures on the Composite Index of blue chip stocks. Its spot May contract last Friday drew heavy volume of 1,965 lots, a far cry from the several hundred contracts a day seen in previous months.
Derivatives, including futures and options contracts, help investors hedge risks in their investments on other markets and can boost returns.

With property concerns dogging countries like Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, and the belief that foreign investors are cutting back on exposure to Asia, currency and shares could stay volatile, further boosting activity on futures exchanges, analysts said.

"People have slowly come round to the view that Asia is not the only growth story or emerging market story in the world and that really is starting to take its toll," Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia chairman Gary Coull told Reuters this week.

Turbulence in the region's markets has sent "a clear message that risk is something real", especially as countries like Malaysia allow a freer flow of capital, Mohd Azwar Mahmud, general manager of Malaysia Monetary Exchange (MME), told the derivatives conference.
The year-old MME, which trades futures on the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR), saw a record-setting 1,393 contracts valued at 1.4 billion ringgit ($560 million) last Friday.

Managed futures funds -- mutual funds of futures and other derivatives -- are also becoming more common throughout the region as investors seek risk control, said Yeong Wai Cheong, principal of Drapeau Advisors Inc in Singapore.

Yeong, who spoke at the derivatives conference, said Thailand's financial community had pooled $1 million each to set up a futures fund -- a kind of mutual fund of futures and other derivatives -- and a similar $75 million fund had been launched in South Korea.
"This industry is on a growth path," he said.
Asia's futures players would be joined by newcomers from the Philippines, Thailand and Indonesia, said Bruce Bradshaw, director of Ord Minett Jardine Fleming in Sydney.
But the nascent derivatives markets could learn a few lessons from older exchanges, he said.

He said the 17-year-old Sydney futures exchange became "arrogant" after charting 30 percent growth annually for nine years, until the Barings derivatives scandal and steady interest rates sent volume plummeting in 1994.
